subject: Science
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 14 periods = 560 minutes
Total: 14 periods · 9h 20min

periods.activity_title: Luminous or Not? Sorting the World Around Us
periods.activity_description: Students examine a curated list of objects from the chapter — Sun, Moon, candle, electric bulb, table, glow-worm, book — and sort them into luminous and non-luminous categories by deciding whether each object produces its own light or merely reflects it.

roles.role_description: Introduces the chapter's opening scenario of Reza's shadow puppet show, then presents the object list and prompts students to articulate their sorting criterion.
Collaboratively sort the object list, record their classifications, and share the reasoning behind any objects the group found difficult to classify.

time_bands.activity: Teacher narrates the opening scenario — Reza and her grandmother noticing how the shadow of a hand changes near the diya — and poses the question: which objects in that scene produce light and which do not?
Groups work through the chapter's object list, classifying each item and writing a one-phrase justification beside each entry in their record sheet.
Groups share their classifications; the class negotiates any disagreements, with the teacher drawing out the criterion of self-produced versus reflected light.

Teacher closes by briefly introducing the bioluminescence fact box — deep-sea fish, fireflies, and bacteria that produce light chemically — as an intriguing boundary case that confirms the luminous category.

periods.teacher_notes: This is the chapter's opening unit, so orient students to the full journey ahead: they will move from classifying light sources to explaining how light travels, and eventually to verifying how it reflects. Watch for students who place the Moon in the luminous category — this is the most common error in this section, and the Moon example from the chapter is the right corrective. A quick show-of-hands checkpoint on the Moon before closing will reveal how many students still hold that misconception.
materials: Printed or board-written object list from Activity 11.1

periods.activity_title: Three Cards, One Flame: Tracing the Path of Light
periods.activity_description: Students set up the three-cardboard-sheet investigation from Activity 11.2, aligning the holes to see a candle flame and then displacing one card to make it disappear, building the claim that light can only travel in a straight line.

roles.role_description: Frames the inquiry question — does light bend or travel straight? — and guides groups through the setup and the deliberate misalignment step.
Construct the three-card arrangement, observe the flame through aligned and misaligned holes, and record what they see in each configuration.

time_bands.activity: Building on the previous unit's conclusion that some objects produce light, the teacher poses the new question: once light is produced, how does it move through space?

Groups set up three cardboard sheets with holes in alignment, observe the candle flame through all three holes, then shift one card and record the result; they repeat the shift with each of the three cards in turn.
Groups write a one-sentence claim based on their observations and share it aloud; the class converges on the pattern that the flame disappears whenever any hole is out of line.

Teacher introduces the term rectilinear propagation of light and shows how a ray of light is represented as a straight line with an arrowhead, connecting the diagram to the card experiment just completed.

periods.teacher_notes: The previous unit established what objects produce light; this unit asks how that light moves. The most important misconception to intercept here is that light fans out or curves around corners — students sometimes expect to see at least a dim glow even when the cards are misaligned. Encourage groups to try the misalignment at different amounts so they see clearly that even a small shift eliminates the flame entirely.
materials: Three cardboard sheets each with a small hole
Table or stand to hold cards upright

periods.activity_title: Straight Tube, Bent Tube: Confirming Light's Path
periods.activity_description: Students direct a torch beam through a straight hollow tube and then through a bent tube, observing that light exits the straight tube but not the bent one, consolidating the rectilinear propagation principle and representing it with ray diagrams.

roles.role_description: Manages the darkened-room condition if possible and prompts students to predict the bent-tube outcome before they test it.
Each student independently draws a ray diagram showing why light passes through the straight tube and why it cannot exit the bent tube, labelling the ray and its direction.

time_bands.activity: Brief recap of the previous unit's three-card result; the teacher sets up the prediction challenge — what will happen when a torch shines through a bent tube?
Groups take turns testing the straight tube and bent tube with a torch, observing whether light emerges, and recording their observations alongside their initial prediction.

Each student independently draws two ray diagrams — one for the straight tube and one for the bent tube — using the arrowhead convention introduced in the previous unit, annotating why light exits or does not exit.
Paired peer review of diagrams; the teacher circulates to confirm that arrows show direction and that the bent-tube diagram correctly shows light stopping at the bend rather than continuing.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit extends the previous unit's card experiment to a different apparatus, so the rectilinear propagation claim is now supported by two independent lines of evidence — a productive scientific habit to name explicitly. A common drawing error is showing the light ray making a turn inside the bent tube; if you spot this, ask the student what would have to be true about light's nature for that to happen, then redirect them to the observation.
materials: Straight hollow tube (e.g. pipe or rolled cardboard)
Bent hollow tube or flexible tube bent into a curve

periods.stage_label: Classify materials and explain shadow formation
periods.activity_title: What Does Light Pass Through? Testing Transparency
periods.activity_description: Students place various classroom materials — clear glass, wood, cardboard, frosted or translucent plastic, thin cloth — in the path of a torch beam and classify each as transparent, translucent, or opaque based on how clearly objects behind each material can be seen.

roles.role_description: Draws attention to the variation in shadow darkness and clarity across materials, prompting students to articulate what is different about each case.
Systematically test each material, record their observations in a three-column classification table, and discuss boundary cases such as thin cloth or a plastic bag.

time_bands.activity: The teacher connects this unit to rectilinear propagation: since light travels straight, an object that blocks it must cast a dark region — what determines how dark or complete that shadow is?

Groups test each material from the chapter's Activity 11.5 list against a torch beam, record whether objects behind the material are clearly visible, blurry, or invisible, and enter results in the classification table.
Groups share results and the class builds a consensus three-column table on the board; the teacher introduces the terms transparent, translucent, and opaque and maps them to the observed categories.

Teacher highlights the boundary cases — thin cloth and plastic bags — where students may disagree, reinforcing that the criterion is clarity of the image behind, not merely the presence of some transmitted light.

periods.teacher_notes: The first two stages established that light travels straight; this unit connects that fact to what happens when materials of different types are placed in light's path. The most common classification error is placing translucent materials in the opaque category because 'you can't see through them clearly' — redirect students to the three-way criterion from the chapter: all through (transparent), some through but blurry (translucent), none through (opaque). Frosted glass and butter paper are the canonical translucent examples to use if disagreement persists.
materials: Clear glass or transparent plastic sheet

periods.stage_label: Classify materials and explain shadow formation
periods.activity_title: Bigger, Smaller: How Distance Shapes a Shadow
periods.activity_description: Students use a torch to cast the shadow of a hand on a wall (Activity 11.4), systematically varying the distance between the hand and the light source and between the hand and the wall, measuring and recording the resulting changes in shadow size.

roles.role_description: Connects the activity to the chapter's opening scenario — Reza noticing her puppet's shadow change size — and prompts students to identify which variable they are changing in each trial.
Conduct multiple trials varying object-to-source and object-to-screen distances, record shadow dimensions, and describe the pattern in words.

time_bands.activity: Teacher recalls Reza's observation from the chapter's opening story and asks: what exactly changes when Reza moves her hand closer to the diya?
Groups set up the torch-and-wall arrangement, conduct trials varying the hand's distance from the torch while keeping the wall fixed, and record shadow size for each position.
Groups vary the second dimension — keeping the torch fixed and moving the hand closer to or farther from the wall — and record the new shadow sizes.

Class shares results and the teacher guides students to state the pattern: closer to the source makes the shadow larger; closer to the screen makes the shadow smaller — and connects this to the straight-line travel of light established in the previous stage.

periods.teacher_notes: The previous unit classified materials; this unit uses that framework to explain why opaque objects produce shadows and then investigates what controls shadow size. Watch for groups that move both variables simultaneously — redirect them to change one factor at a time and explain why that matters for drawing a reliable conclusion. Connecting the shadow size pattern explicitly to rectilinear propagation (light rays spreading from a point source in straight lines) deepens the causal explanation.
materials: White wall or large white paper sheet as screen

periods.stage_label: Construct and explain the pinhole camera
periods.activity_description: Students construct a pinhole camera from two nested cardboard boxes — one with a pinhole and the other with a translucent screen — following Activity 11.6, then point it at a bright outdoor scene or lamp and observe the image formed.

roles.role_description: Demonstrates the assembly sequence and ensures all groups produce a light-tight sliding fit between the two boxes before they observe.
Construct the pinhole camera, point it at a bright source, slide the inner box to focus, and sketch the image they observe on the screen.

time_bands.activity: Building on shadow formation from the previous stage, the teacher poses a new question: can a tiny hole form an actual image of an object, and if so, what kind of image?

Groups construct the two-box pinhole camera — making the pinhole on the closed face of the outer box and the translucent screen on the open inner box — and observe a bright source, adjusting the sliding distance to sharpen the image.
Groups sketch the image they observe, noting its orientation compared to the actual object, and record whether the image appears upright or inverted.
Teacher asks groups to share their sketches and collects observations about image orientation, setting up the explanation activity in the next unit.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit introduces the pinhole camera as a physical consequence of rectilinear propagation — a key conceptual bridge. Students often expect the image to be upright because that is how they see the world through their eyes; when it is inverted, they are surprised and ready to ask why. Hold the explanation for the next unit so that this unit is purely observational — let the surprise do pedagogical work. Ensure the pinhole is genuinely small (a pin-width); a large hole produces a blurry patch, not a clear inverted image.
materials: Two cardboard boxes of slightly different sizes (one sliding inside the other)
Tracing paper or translucent plastic sheet for screen
Pin or needle for making pinhole
Candle or bright lamp as light source

periods.stage_label: Construct and explain the pinhole camera
periods.activity_title: Why the Image Is Upside Down: Tracing the Rays
periods.activity_description: Students draw a ray diagram showing how light from the top and bottom of an object travels in straight lines through the pinhole and arrives at the opposite positions on the screen, explaining the inverted image, and connect this to the historical camera obscura.

roles.role_description: Walks students through the ray-tracing logic step by step, using a board diagram, then invites students to reproduce it independently.
Draw the ray diagram from scratch — labelling object, pinhole, screen, top ray, and bottom ray — and write a one-sentence explanation of why the image is inverted.

time_bands.activity: Teacher recalls groups' sketches from the previous unit and asks: since light travels in straight lines, which direction does the ray from the top of the object travel after passing through the pinhole?

Teacher constructs the ray diagram on the board step by step — object on the left, pinhole in the centre, screen on the right — tracing the top ray to the bottom of the screen and vice versa, narrating the logic at each step.
Each student independently draws the complete ray diagram in their notebook, labelling all components, and writes the one-sentence causal explanation.
Teacher introduces the camera obscura from the chapter's fact box — a room-sized pinhole camera used by artists — connecting the principle to the device students just built and to early photography.

periods.teacher_notes: The previous unit produced the surprising observation; this unit supplies the causal explanation rooted in rectilinear propagation. Students frequently draw the two rays crossing at the screen rather than at the pinhole — if you see this, ask them where the rays first meet and why that must be at the hole, not somewhere else. Linking the camera obscura story to the device students built in the previous unit gives the historical fact genuine meaning rather than making it feel like an isolated curiosity.
materials: Board and chalk or whiteboard markers
homework: Draw a second ray diagram in which the object is moved closer to the pinhole and predict whether the image on the screen becomes larger or smaller, explaining your prediction using the straight-line travel of light.

periods.stage_label: Observe and describe reflection of light
periods.activity_title: Bouncing Light: First Encounter with Reflection
periods.activity_description: Students direct a torch beam at a plane mirror in a darkened room and observe a reflected beam on an adjacent wall (Activity 11.7), then compare the reflected beam from a mirror with what happens when the same beam strikes a rough or matte surface.

roles.role_description: Darkens the room sufficiently for the reflected beam to be visible and prompts students to describe what the reflected beam has in common with and what differs from the incident beam.
Direct the torch at the mirror and at a rough surface in turn, record observations about the reflected beam's clarity and direction for each surface, and write a comparative statement.

time_bands.activity: Teacher bridges from the pinhole camera stage: so far we know light travels straight and can form images — now a new question arises from the opening story: what happens when light strikes a surface and bounces back?
Groups direct the torch at the mirror, observing the reflected beam on the wall; they record the beam's position and clarity, then repeat with a rough matte surface and record the contrast.
Groups share their comparative statements; the class agrees that smooth surfaces produce a clear, directed reflected beam while rough surfaces scatter light without a clear beam.
Teacher introduces the term reflection and connects the everyday examples from the chapter — still water, polished metal surfaces — to the observation groups just made.

periods.teacher_notes: This is the opening unit of the reflection stage, and it moves from the pinhole camera's use of rectilinear propagation to a new behaviour of light — reflection. Students sometimes confuse scattering from rough surfaces with absorption; clarify that rough surfaces still reflect light but in many directions at once, which is why there is no single clear beam. The contrast between mirror and rough surface in a single activity makes this distinction visceral rather than abstract.
materials: Rough or matte white cardboard surface

periods.stage_label: Observe and describe reflection of light
periods.activity_title: Measuring the Angles: Discovering the Laws of Reflection
periods.activity_description: Students systematically direct a ray of light at a plane mirror at various angles (Activity 11.8), trace incident and reflected rays on paper, draw the normal, measure both angles with a protractor, and tabulate results to identify the pattern relating angle of incidence and angle of reflection.

roles.role_description: Introduces the vocabulary — incident ray, reflected ray, normal, angle of incidence, angle of reflection — and demonstrates the tracing procedure once before groups begin.
Conduct at least four trials at different angles, trace rays, draw the normal, measure both angles, record results in a table, and write the pattern they observe.

time_bands.activity: Building on the previous unit's qualitative observation, the teacher asks whether there is a precise, measurable relationship between the incoming and outgoing beam, introduces the normal and the two angle definitions, and demonstrates one tracing trial.

Groups conduct multiple trials at different incident angles, tracing rays on paper placed under or beside the mirror, drawing the normal at the point of incidence, and measuring both angles with a protractor.
Groups enter results in a shared table format and identify the numerical pattern; they write the first law of reflection in their own words from their data.
Teacher formalises both laws — equal angles, and coplanarity of incident ray, normal, and reflected ray — and connects them to the data in the groups' tables.

periods.teacher_notes: The previous unit established that reflection exists and that smooth surfaces produce a directed beam; this unit moves from qualitative observation to quantitative measurement and formal law derivation. The most frequent measurement error is students measuring the angle from the mirror surface rather than from the normal — demonstrate once with a protractor on the board to make the normal reference line explicit. Having groups share their angle tables openly helps students see that the equal-angle law holds across many different incident angles, not just for special cases.

periods.stage_label: Investigate image properties in a plane mirror
periods.activity_title: Locating the Image: Pin Method with a Plane Mirror
periods.activity_description: Students use the two-pin method from Activity 11.9 — placing one pin as object and using a second pin to locate the position where the image appears — measuring object distance and image distance from the mirror surface and noting size correspondence.

roles.role_description: Demonstrates the pin-coincidence technique for locating the image and ensures students understand they are finding the apparent position of the image, not a physical object behind the mirror.
Set up the pin and mirror arrangement, find the image position by the coincidence method, measure and record both distances, and repeat with the object at a different distance.

time_bands.activity: Teacher connects to the laws of reflection established in the previous unit and poses the image question: if reflected rays seem to come from behind the mirror, where exactly does the image appear to be?

Groups place the object pin in front of the mirror, use the second pin behind the mirror to find the position where it coincides with the image of the first pin, and measure the object and image distances from the mirror.
Groups repeat with the object at a second, different distance and record results in a two-column table of object distance versus image distance.

Class compiles results; teacher draws out the pattern — image distance equals object distance — and asks groups whether the image can be caught on a screen, setting up the virtual image concept for the next unit.

periods.teacher_notes: The previous stage established how reflection works; this unit begins investigating what that reflection produces — an image. Students may try to place the second pin anywhere behind the mirror rather than using the coincidence criterion; insist on the parallax-free coincidence method from the activity to ensure accuracy. The equal-distance result prepares students for the virtual image definition, so hold that formal term until the next unit where it is introduced alongside lateral inversion.
materials: Two identical pins or thin sticks
Soft board or thick cardboard to hold pins

periods.stage_label: Investigate image properties in a plane mirror
periods.activity_title: Virtual, Upright, Laterally Inverted: Characterising the Mirror Image
periods.activity_description: Students write text in front of a plane mirror (Activity 11.10), observe lateral inversion, then attempt to project the mirror image onto a screen placed behind the mirror, confirming it cannot be projected and introducing the definition of a virtual image.

roles.role_description: Connects the AMBULANCE example from the chapter to lateral inversion and asks students to predict what any word would look like in the mirror before they test it.

Write a short word in front of the mirror, sketch the mirror image, attempt to project it onto a screen behind the mirror, and record all three image properties — distance, size, and lateral inversion — in a summary statement.

time_bands.activity: Teacher recalls the equal-distance result from the previous unit and asks: besides position, what other properties does the mirror image have — can it be projected, and does it look exactly the same as the object?
Each student writes a word in front of the mirror, sketches what they see, and attempts to catch the image on a screen held behind the mirror, recording whether it is possible.

Class shares sketches; teacher introduces the term virtual image and explains why it cannot be formed on a screen — reflected rays appear to diverge from a point behind the mirror but never actually converge there.

Teacher introduces lateral inversion using the AMBULANCE example from the chapter and connects it to the word-in-mirror observation, then summarises all three plane mirror image properties in a class-generated table.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit completes the plane mirror investigation begun in the previous unit by adding the virtual image concept and lateral inversion. Students frequently believe that because the image looks real and is the same size it should be projectable; letting them actually attempt to catch it on a screen makes the virtual image definition concrete rather than definitional. The AMBULANCE example is in the chapter and is a powerful hook — ask students to suggest other real-world applications of the same principle before moving on.
materials: Paper and pen for writing text

periods.stage_label: Demonstrate and verify behaviour of light through systematic manipulation of apparatus
periods.activity_title: Two Mirrors, Many Images: Exploring Multiple Reflections
periods.activity_description: Students place an object between two plane mirrors held at various angles (Activity 11.11) and count the number of images formed at each angle, establishing the relationship between angle and image count, and exploring the limiting case of parallel mirrors.

roles.role_description: Prompts students to predict the number of images before each angular setting and to consider what happens to image count as the angle approaches zero.
Set the mirrors at each specified angle, count images carefully, record angle-versus-image-count data in a table, and describe what happens as the mirrors approach parallel alignment.

time_bands.activity: Teacher connects to the single plane mirror image from the previous two units and poses the question: if one mirror produces one image, what do two mirrors at an angle produce — and why?
Groups place the object between mirrors at several different angles, count images at each setting, and fill in an angle-versus-image-count data table.
Groups bring mirrors progressively closer to parallel and describe what happens to the image count, noting the 'very large' result for parallel mirrors mentioned in the chapter.
Teacher introduces the kaleidoscope as a direct application of multiple reflections — three mirrors in a triangular prism arrangement — and previews the construction activity in the next unit.

periods.teacher_notes: The single-mirror work of the previous two units is now extended to two mirrors, elevating the demand from characterising a single image to reasoning about the geometry of repeated reflections. Students often miscount images by including the object itself or by counting a single image twice from different viewing angles; encourage groups to move their eye position and verify that the count stays constant. The parallel-mirror limiting case is conceptually important and also intrinsically engaging — let groups experience the 'corridor of images' effect before you name it.

periods.stage_label: Demonstrate and verify behaviour of light through systematic manipulation of apparatus
periods.activity_title: Constructing a Kaleidoscope: Multiple Reflections in Action
periods.activity_description: Students construct a simple kaleidoscope using three mirrors arranged in a triangular prism, place coloured beads or paper pieces at one end, observe the symmetrical patterns produced by multiple reflections, and connect the pattern geometry to the equal-angle law and the multiple-reflection principle.

roles.role_description: Guides the assembly sequence and asks students to predict the symmetry of the pattern before they look, connecting the prediction to the number-of-images principle from the previous unit.

Assemble the three-mirror prism, insert coloured materials, observe and sketch two different patterns, and write a sentence connecting the pattern symmetry to the laws of reflection and multiple reflections.

time_bands.activity: Teacher recalls the multiple-reflection data from the previous unit and asks: the kaleidoscope uses three mirrors at 60° — based on our data, how many images would you expect, and what symmetry does that produce?

Groups assemble the kaleidoscope — three mirror strips taped into a triangular prism, one end open for materials and the other for the eye — insert coloured beads or paper, and observe and sketch two different patterns.
Groups write the connecting sentence between pattern symmetry, the number of images from the multiple-reflection investigation, and the laws of reflection established in the earlier stage.

Teacher introduces the periscope from the chapter's Fascinating Facts box — two plane mirrors at 45° allowing observation over obstacles — as a second device using multiple reflections, and asks students where they have seen periscopes used.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit synthesises multiple reflections with the laws of reflection by having students build a functional optical device. The most common assembly error is mirrors arranged with the reflective face pointing outward rather than inward; check this before groups begin observing or the pattern will not form. Asking students to write the connecting sentence — linking pattern symmetry to the laws of reflection — is the key cognitive move that elevates this from a craft activity to a demonstration of understanding.
materials: Three rectangular mirror strips of equal size
Coloured beads or small pieces of coloured paper or cellophane
Translucent plastic or tracing paper for end cap

periods.stage_label: Demonstrate and verify behaviour of light through systematic manipulation of apparatus
periods.activity_title: Putting It All Together: Verifying Propagation and Reflection with Evidence
periods.activity_description: Students are presented with a set of optical scenarios drawn from the chapter — pinhole camera image orientation, shadow size change, mirror image location, angle-of-incidence equality — and must select the correct apparatus arrangement and predict the outcome for each, justifying every prediction using the rectilinear propagation principle or the laws of reflection.

roles.role_description: Presents each scenario as a challenge question and circulates to probe the reasoning behind each group's apparatus choice and prediction rather than confirming or denying answers.
Discuss and agree on the apparatus arrangement and predicted outcome for each scenario, then select one scenario to physically demonstrate to the class, explaining their reasoning aloud.

time_bands.activity: Teacher sets the context: across this chapter students have built, measured, and observed — this unit asks them to reason from principles to new predictions using the full toolkit they have developed.
Groups work through the scenario set, agreeing on apparatus arrangement and predicted outcome for each and recording their reasoning in terms of rectilinear propagation or the laws of reflection.
Each group selects one scenario to physically demonstrate to the class, presenting the apparatus setup, stated prediction, and observed result, with the teacher probing the causal reasoning.

Teacher closes by naming the two principles that underpin every scenario — rectilinear propagation and the laws of reflection — and notes that the devices built across the chapter are all demonstrations of these two principles working together.

periods.teacher_notes: This closing unit draws the whole chapter together by requiring students to apply both major principles — rectilinear propagation and the laws of reflection — to unfamiliar scenario descriptions, which is the highest cognitive operation the chapter targets. Watch for groups that identify the correct apparatus but cannot articulate the causal principle; prompt them with 'why does that arrangement produce that result?' rather than supplying the answer. The physical demonstration step ensures that reasoning is grounded in actual observation rather than recalled answers.
materials: Pinhole camera from the earlier unit if available
Two plane mirrors for multiple-reflection scenario

coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students classify a set of objects as luminous or non-luminous by deciding whether each produces its own light, including boundary cases such as bioluminescent organisms.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can sort a given set of objects into luminous and non-luminous categories and justify each classification with a criterion drawn from whether the object produces or only reflects light.

coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students use the three-card alignment activity and the straight-versus-bent tube activity to build and confirm the claim that light travels in straight lines, representing the result with ray diagrams.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can describe evidence from two independent investigations that light travels in straight lines and represent this with correctly labelled ray diagrams showing direction of travel.

coverage_handoff.stage_label: Classify materials and explain shadow formation
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students classify materials as transparent, translucent, or opaque based on light transmission observations, and investigate how varying object-to-source and object-to-screen distances changes shadow size, connecting the pattern causally to rectilinear propagation.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can classify materials as transparent, translucent, or opaque and explain how shadow size changes when an opaque object is moved relative to a light source or screen, using the straight-line travel of light as the causal mechanism.

coverage_handoff.stage_label: Construct and explain the pinhole camera
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students construct a pinhole camera, observe and sketch the inverted image it forms, then draw ray diagrams tracing light from top and bottom of the object through the pinhole to show why the image is inverted.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can construct a functional pinhole camera, observe the inverted image it produces, and explain image inversion using a ray diagram that traces rectilinear propagation through the pinhole.

coverage_handoff.stage_label: Observe and describe reflection of light
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students observe reflected beams from mirror and rough surfaces, then systematically measure angles of incidence and reflection across multiple trials to identify and state the two laws of reflection from their own data.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can state the two laws of reflection and support each law with measured angle data from their own investigation, correctly identifying the normal, incident ray, and reflected ray.

coverage_handoff.stage_label: Investigate image properties in a plane mirror
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students use the two-pin method to locate the mirror image and measure its distance, then characterise the image as virtual, same-size, and laterally inverted through a text-in-mirror observation and a screen-projection attempt.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can locate the image formed by a plane mirror using the pin method, measure object and image distances, and describe the image as virtual, upright, same-size, and laterally inverted with observational evidence for each property.

coverage_handoff.stage_label: Demonstrate and verify behaviour of light through systematic manipulation of apparatus
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students investigate multiple reflections between two mirrors at varying angles, construct a kaleidoscope connecting the device's symmetry to the laws of reflection, and then apply both the rectilinear propagation principle and the laws of reflection to a set of optical scenarios, predicting and physically demonstrating outcomes.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can demonstrate that light travels in straight lines and verify the laws of reflection by manipulating light sources, mirrors, and optical apparatus — including pinhole cameras, plane mirrors, and kaleidoscopes — and justify each predicted outcome using the appropriate physical principle.

assessment_items.stage_label: Observe and classify light sources
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can sort a given set of objects into luminous and non-luminous categories and justify each classification with a criterion drawn from whether the object produces or only reflects light.

competency.competency_text: Demonstrating rectilinear propagation of light from different sources and verifying the laws of reflection through manipulation of light sources and objects and the use of apparatus and artefacts such as plane mirrors, pinhole camera, kaleidoscope, and periscope.

assessment_items.question_text: A student lists four objects: the Moon, a burning candle, a glass table, and a firefly. Which two objects belong to the same category because of how they relate to light?

options.label: A
options.text: The burning candle and the firefly, because both are small light sources.

options.label: B
options.text: The firefly and the glass table, because both involve living things or transparent materials.

options.label: C
options.text: The Moon and the burning candle, because both are visible at night.

options.label: D
options.text: The Moon and the glass table, because neither produces its own light.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing this option indicates the student is classifying by apparent similarity (both are small) rather than by the luminous/non-luminous criterion; it conflates size with light production.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Choosing this option shows the student is using a context-based criterion (night visibility) rather than the self-production-of-light criterion, a common misconception driven by everyday experience.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Choosing this option reveals category confusion — the student is mixing unrelated properties (biology, transparency) rather than applying the single criterion of whether the object produces its own light.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who struggle with written classification may be invited to sort physical cards with object names or pictures into two labelled groups. Students who classify quickly and correctly can be asked to identify one additional object from the classroom that belongs to each category and justify it.

assessment_items.stage_label: Observe and classify light sources
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can sort a given set of objects into luminous and non-luminous categories and justify each classification with a criterion drawn from whether the object produces or only reflects light.

competency.competency_text: Demonstrating rectilinear propagation of light from different sources and verifying the laws of reflection through manipulation of light sources and objects and the use of apparatus and artefacts such as plane mirrors, pinhole camera, kaleidoscope, and periscope.

assessment_items.question_text: An anglerfish living in the deep sea produces its own light through chemical reactions in its body. Which statement correctly classifies the anglerfish?

options.label: A
options.text: It is luminous because it produces its own light through chemical reactions.

options.label: B
options.text: It is non-luminous because fish do not have electricity to power a bulb.

options.label: C
options.text: It is non-luminous because it lives in the dark and cannot reflect sunlight.

options.label: D
options.text: It is translucent because light passes through its body.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Choosing this option indicates the student is linking luminous/non-luminous to sunlight availability, confusing the classification criterion (self-production) with an environmental condition.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Choosing this option reveals a misconception that luminous objects require an electrical mechanism; the student has not engaged with the bioluminescence content from the chapter.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing this option shows the student has confused the luminous/non-luminous classification with the transparent/translucent/opaque classification system, conflating two separate frameworks from the chapter.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students unfamiliar with the term 'bioluminescence' can still answer by applying the definitional criterion — does it produce its own light? — which the question stem states directly. Teachers may allow students to underline the key phrase in the stem before answering.

assessment_items.stage_label: Investigate and establish rectilinear propagation
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can describe evidence from two independent investigations that light travels in straight lines and represent this with correctly labelled ray diagrams showing direction of travel.

competency.competency_text: Demonstrating rectilinear propagation of light from different sources and verifying the laws of reflection through manipulation of light sources and objects and the use of apparatus and artefacts such as plane mirrors, pinhole camera, kaleidoscope, and periscope.

assessment_items.question_text: In the three-card experiment, a candle flame is clearly visible when the holes in all three cards are aligned. A student shifts the middle card sideways by a small amount. What will the student observe, and why?

options.label: A
options.text: The flame disappears, because the card absorbs all the light from the candle.

options.label: B
options.text: The flame disappears, because the shifted card blocks the straight-line path of light from the candle to the eye.

options.label: C
options.text: The flame remains visible because air gaps between the cards allow light to pass through.

options.label: D
options.text: The flame remains visible but appears dimmer, because light bends slightly around the edge of the card.

what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing this option reveals the core misconception that light bends around edges — exactly the alternative conception the three-card activity is designed to challenge.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing this option shows the student understands the flame disappears but attributes it to absorption rather than to the broken straight-line alignment, indicating a gap in causal reasoning about rectilinear propagation.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Choosing this option indicates the student has not engaged with the experimental logic: the shift of any card breaks the straight-line path regardless of air gaps, which this response ignores.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who found the written explanation challenging can be invited to draw the card arrangement and mark the light path to justify their answer visually. Students who answer quickly can be asked to predict what would happen if the card were shifted vertically rather than horizontally.

assessment_items.stage_label: Investigate and establish rectilinear propagation
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can describe evidence from two independent investigations that light travels in straight lines and represent this with correctly labelled ray diagrams showing direction of travel.

competency.competency_text: Demonstrating rectilinear propagation of light from different sources and verifying the laws of reflection through manipulation of light sources and objects and the use of apparatus and artefacts such as plane mirrors, pinhole camera, kaleidoscope, and periscope.

assessment_items.question_text: A student shines a torch through a straight hollow tube and light appears at the other end. The student then bends the tube into a curve and shines the torch again. Which option correctly describes the outcome and gives the right reason?

options.label: A
options.text: Light appears at the far end of the bent tube because light always finds a path through any hollow space.

options.label: B
options.text: Light appears at the far end of the bent tube, but it is weaker because it loses energy at the bend.

options.label: C
options.text: No light appears at the far end of the bent tube, because light travels only in straight lines and cannot follow the curve.

options.label: D
options.text: No light appears at the far end of the bent tube, because the tube material absorbs light when bent.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Choosing this option reveals the misconception that light can bend but is weakened; the student has not accepted that the direction constraint (straight line) is absolute, not a matter of degree.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing this option shows the student identifies the correct observation (no light) but attributes the cause to material absorption rather than the rectilinear propagation principle, indicating incomplete causal reasoning.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing this option indicates the student holds the alternative conception that light can navigate any hollow path, directly contradicting the rectilinear propagation principle.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who struggle with the written scenario may benefit from the teacher briefly miming the two tube setups before the student answers. Students who demonstrate the correct reasoning can be asked to draw the corresponding ray diagram to extend their response.

assessment_items.stage_label: Investigate and establish rectilinear propagation
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can describe evidence from two independent investigations that light travels in straight lines and represent this with correctly labelled ray diagrams showing direction of travel.

competency.competency_text: Demonstrating rectilinear propagation of light from different sources and verifying the laws of reflection through manipulation of light sources and objects and the use of apparatus and artefacts such as plane mirrors, pinhole camera, kaleidoscope, and periscope.

assessment_items.question_text: Draw a ray diagram for a torch shining through a straight hollow tube. Label the light source, the tube, and the ray. Show the arrowhead on the ray. Then explain in one sentence why the same torch produces no light at the far end when the tube is bent.
expected_elements: A diagram showing a torch (or labelled light source) at one end of a straight tube and a ray drawn as a straight line with an arrowhead pointing away from the source toward the far end.
Labels identifying the light source, tube, and ray.
A one-sentence explanation that attributes the failure in the bent tube to light travelling only in straight lines — not to material absorption or energy loss.

SCR.inclusivity: Students who find drawing difficult may describe the diagram in words, provided they identify the positions of source, tube, and ray and state the direction. Students who complete this quickly can be asked to add a second diagram for the bent tube showing where the ray stops and why.

assessment_items.stage_label: Classify materials and explain shadow formation
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can classify materials as transparent, translucent, or opaque and explain how shadow size changes when an opaque object is moved relative to a light source or screen, using the straight-line travel of light as the causal mechanism.

competency.competency_text: Demonstrating rectilinear propagation of light from different sources and verifying the laws of reflection through manipulation of light sources and objects and the use of apparatus and artefacts such as plane mirrors, pinhole camera, kaleidoscope, and periscope.

assessment_items.visual_stimulus:
Material | Observation when torch shines through it
Frosted glass | Objects behind it appear blurry
Clear glass | Objects behind it are clearly visible
Wood | No light passes through; no objects visible behind it
Thin cloth | Objects behind it are faintly visible but not clear
assessment_items.question_text: Refer to the table provided. Which row contains a material that does NOT belong to the same classification category as frosted glass?

options.label: A
options.text: Clear glass, because objects behind it are clearly visible, placing it in a different category from frosted glass.

options.label: B
options.text: Thin cloth, because it allows some light through but objects behind it are not clearly visible.

options.label: C
options.text: Wood, because it allows no light through, which is slightly different from frosted glass that allows some light.

options.label: D
options.text: Wood, because it is a natural material and frosted glass is manufactured.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Choosing this option shows the student has not distinguished between translucent and transparent: thin cloth, like frosted glass, scatters light so objects appear blurry — both are translucent — but the student has classified thin cloth as different from frosted glass.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing this option shows the student is classifying by material origin (natural vs. manufactured) rather than by the optical criterion of how much and how clearly light passes through.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Choosing this option reveals a productive partial understanding — the student correctly identifies that wood transmits no light — but attributes the difference to degree of transmission rather than to the category boundary between opaque and translucent.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who struggle to read the table may have the teacher read each row aloud. Students who finish quickly can be asked to add a fifth row to the table with a material of their own choice and classify it, justifying their entry.

assessment_items.stage_label: Classify materials and explain shadow formation
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can classify materials as transparent, translucent, or opaque and explain how shadow size changes when an opaque object is moved relative to a light source or screen, using the straight-line travel of light as the causal mechanism.

competency.competency_text: Demonstrating rectilinear propagation of light from different sources and verifying the laws of reflection through manipulation of light sources and objects and the use of apparatus and artefacts such as plane mirrors, pinhole camera, kaleidoscope, and periscope.

assessment_items.question_text: Reza holds her hand between a diya and a wall. She then moves her hand closer to the diya, keeping the wall in the same position. What happens to the shadow on the wall, and what causes this change?

options.label: A
options.text: The shadow gets larger, because moving the hand closer to the light source means the straight rays of light that the hand intercepts spread out over a larger area of the wall.

options.label: B
options.text: The shadow gets larger, because the hand now reflects more light toward the wall.

options.label: C
options.text: The shadow gets smaller, because the hand is now closer to the light source and blocks less of the room.

options.label: D
options.text: The shadow stays the same size, because the hand has not changed and neither has the wall.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Choosing this option reveals an inverted intuition — the student thinks closer to the source means a smaller shadow — possibly from the real-world experience that moving away from a lamp makes a shadow bigger, which the student has reversed without a causal model.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing this option shows the student has not connected the geometric relationship between source distance and shadow size; the student is treating shadow size as a property of the object alone rather than of the object-source-screen arrangement.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Choosing this option reveals a misconception that the hand is acting as a reflecting surface contributing to the pattern on the wall, rather than as an opaque blocker of straight-travelling rays.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who find the spatial reasoning difficult may be invited to sketch the hand, diya, and wall from a side view before choosing an answer. Students who identify the correct answer can be challenged to predict what would happen if the hand were moved closer to the wall instead.

assessment_items.stage_label: Classify materials and explain shadow formation
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can classify materials as transparent, translucent, or opaque and explain how shadow size changes when an opaque object is moved relative to a light source or screen, using the straight-line travel of light as the causal mechanism.

competency.competency_text: Demonstrating rectilinear propagation of light from different sources and verifying the laws of reflection through manipulation of light sources and objects and the use of apparatus and artefacts such as plane mirrors, pinhole camera, kaleidoscope, and periscope.

assessment_items.question_text: A student uses a torch to cast a shadow of a cardboard cut-out on a wall. The student then moves the cut-out farther from the torch and closer to the wall. Describe what happens to the shadow and explain why, using the idea that light travels in straight lines.
expected_elements: Statement that the shadow becomes smaller (or decreases in size) as the cut-out moves farther from the torch and closer to the wall.

An explanation that connects the change to rectilinear propagation: the straight rays from the torch spread less by the time they reach the cut-out when the cut-out is farther from the source, so the cut-out intercepts a smaller cone of rays, casting a smaller shadow.
Identification of the cut-out as opaque — the cause of any shadow at all.

SCR.inclusivity: Students may draw a side-view diagram alongside their written explanation; a diagram that correctly shows converging or diverging rays relative to the object position can substitute for part of the written causal explanation. Students who complete this quickly can be asked to describe what material the cut-out must be and why a translucent material would produce a different result.

assessment_items.stage_label: Construct and explain the pinhole camera
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can construct a functional pinhole camera, observe the inverted image it produces, and explain image inversion using a ray diagram that traces rectilinear propagation through the pinhole.

competency.competency_text: Demonstrating rectilinear propagation of light from different sources and verifying the laws of reflection through manipulation of light sources and objects and the use of apparatus and artefacts such as plane mirrors, pinhole camera, kaleidoscope, and periscope.

assessment_items.question_text: In a pinhole camera, the image of a tree appears upside down on the screen. Which of the following correctly explains this?

options.label: A
options.text: Light from the top of the tree is stronger and pushes the image to the bottom of the screen.

options.label: B
options.text: Light from the top of the tree travels in a straight line through the pinhole and reaches the bottom of the screen, while light from the bottom of the tree reaches the top of the screen.

options.label: C
options.text: The pinhole bends light downward, so the top of the tree appears at the bottom of the screen.

options.label: D
options.text: The screen material reverses the image because it is translucent, not transparent.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Choosing this option reveals the persistent misconception that the pinhole bends or refracts light; the student has not applied the rectilinear propagation principle from the earlier stage to this new device.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing this option shows the student has attributed image inversion to the screen material rather than to the geometry of straight-line ray crossing at the pinhole, confusing material properties with geometric optics.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing this option indicates the student is reasoning about light intensity or force rather than direction, revealing a fundamental gap in the geometric ray model.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who struggle with the spatial inversion concept may be invited to use their fingers to trace the path from the top and bottom of an imaginary object through a single point (the pinhole) to a wall, experiencing the crossing physically before choosing an answer.

assessment_items.stage_label: Construct and explain the pinhole camera
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can construct a functional pinhole camera, observe the inverted image it produces, and explain image inversion using a ray diagram that traces rectilinear propagation through the pinhole.

competency.competency_text: Demonstrating rectilinear propagation of light from different sources and verifying the laws of reflection through manipulation of light sources and objects and the use of apparatus and artefacts such as plane mirrors, pinhole camera, kaleidoscope, and periscope.

assessment_items.question_text: A student makes a pinhole camera and observes a clear inverted image. The student then makes the pinhole larger. What is likely to happen to the image, and why?

options.label: A
options.text: The image becomes blurry, because a large hole allows rays from many different angles to reach the same point on the screen, smearing the image.

options.label: B
options.text: The image becomes brighter and remains equally sharp, because more light enters through the larger hole.

options.label: C
options.text: The image becomes upright rather than inverted, because the larger hole allows light to bend back.

options.label: D
options.text: The image disappears entirely, because the hole is too large to focus any light.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Choosing this option shows the student understands that a larger hole admits more light (correct) but does not understand that the sharpness of a pinhole image depends on the hole being small enough to act as a single point of entry.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing this option reveals an extreme-case error: the student assumes the image must vanish completely, not realising that a large hole still transmits light — it just produces a blurry patch rather than a clear image.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Choosing this option shows the student has confused hole size with image orientation, re-introducing the bending misconception in a new guise.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who struggle with the concept of blur may be encouraged to think about what happens when multiple slightly different straight-line paths all arrive at the same screen point. Students who answer correctly can be asked to predict whether moving the screen farther from the pinhole would sharpen or blur the image further.

assessment_items.stage_label: Construct and explain the pinhole camera
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can construct a functional pinhole camera, observe the inverted image it produces, and explain image inversion using a ray diagram that traces rectilinear propagation through the pinhole.

competency.competency_text: Demonstrating rectilinear propagation of light from different sources and verifying the laws of reflection through manipulation of light sources and objects and the use of apparatus and artefacts such as plane mirrors, pinhole camera, kaleidoscope, and periscope.

assessment_items.question_text: Draw a ray diagram of a pinhole camera with a lit candle as the object. Your diagram should show: (a) two rays — one from the top of the candle flame and one from the bottom — each passing through the pinhole; (b) where each ray hits the screen; (c) the image formed, showing its orientation. Write one sentence explaining why the image is inverted.
expected_elements: A diagram showing a candle on the left, a pinhole in the centre panel, and a screen on the right.

Two rays drawn as straight lines with arrowheads: one from the top of the candle passing through the pinhole and reaching the bottom of the screen; one from the bottom of the candle passing through the pinhole and reaching the top of the screen.
An inverted image of the candle sketched on the screen (flame at bottom, base at top).
A one-sentence explanation that rays from opposite ends of the object cross at the pinhole because light travels in straight lines, producing an inverted image.

SCR.inclusivity: Students who find drawing challenging may describe the path of each ray in words instead of drawing, specifying where each ray starts, passes through, and ends. Students who complete the diagram quickly can be challenged to add a third ray from the middle of the candle and predict where it arrives on the screen.

assessment_items.stage_label: Observe and describe reflection of light
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can state the two laws of reflection and support each law with measured angle data from their own investigation, correctly identifying the normal, incident ray, and reflected ray.

competency.competency_text: Demonstrating rectilinear propagation of light from different sources and verifying the laws of reflection through manipulation of light sources and objects and the use of apparatus and artefacts such as plane mirrors, pinhole camera, kaleidoscope, and periscope.

assessment_items.visual_stimulus:
Trial | Angle of incidence (degrees) | Angle of reflection (degrees)
1 | 20 | 20
2 | 35 | 35
3 | 50 | 50
4 | 65 | 65
assessment_items.question_text: A student measures the angle of incidence and angle of reflection for four trials. Refer to the table provided. Which conclusion is best supported by this data?

options.label: A
options.text: The angle of incidence and the angle of reflection are measured from the mirror surface, not from the normal.

options.label: B
options.text: The angle of incidence is always equal to the angle of reflection.

options.label: C
options.text: The angle of reflection is always larger than the angle of incidence because the mirror adds energy to the reflected ray.

options.label: D
options.text: The pattern holds only for angles smaller than 45 degrees and breaks down for larger angles.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Choosing this option reveals a misconception about energy addition by the mirror; the student has not read the data pattern and has introduced a physically incorrect causal explanation.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing this option identifies a common procedural error — measuring from the mirror surface rather than from the normal — and the student is claiming this error is the correct method, indicating incomplete understanding of the measurement convention.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing this option shows the student is applying a limited-range interpretation to the data without grounds; trial 4 at 65° already contradicts the claimed cutoff, but the student may not have read the full table.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who find table reading difficult may highlight or circle the matching pairs before choosing a conclusion. Students who identify the correct answer can be asked to state the second law of reflection — about coplanarity — and explain why the data table cannot by itself confirm or deny it.

assessment_items.stage_label: Observe and describe reflection of light
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can state the two laws of reflection and support each law with measured angle data from their own investigation, correctly identifying the normal, incident ray, and reflected ray.

competency.competency_text: Demonstrating rectilinear propagation of light from different sources and verifying the laws of reflection through manipulation of light sources and objects and the use of apparatus and artefacts such as plane mirrors, pinhole camera, kaleidoscope, and periscope.

assessment_items.question_text: In a reflection diagram, the incident ray strikes a plane mirror at a point. The normal is drawn at that point. The angle of incidence is 40 degrees. Which statement about the reflected ray is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: The reflected ray makes an angle of 40 degrees with the mirror surface.

options.label: B
options.text: The reflected ray makes an angle of 40 degrees with the normal, on the opposite side of the normal from the incident ray.

options.label: C
options.text: The reflected ray makes an angle of 50 degrees with the normal, because the mirror deflects the ray by an additional 10 degrees.

options.label: D
options.text: The reflected ray travels back along exactly the same path as the incident ray, because both angles must be equal.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing this option reveals the most common measurement error in this topic: measuring from the mirror surface rather than from the normal, so the student has calculated the complementary angle (90 - 40 = 50) or has simply conflated surface angle and normal angle.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Choosing this option shows the student has the right reference line (the normal) but has applied an incorrect numerical modification, possibly confusing angle of incidence with angle of deviation.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing this option reveals a partial understanding: the student knows both angles are equal and correctly concludes equal angles, but interprets this to mean the ray reverses — true only for 0-degree incidence, not for 40 degrees.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who struggle with visualising the geometry may be allowed to sketch the mirror, normal, and rays before answering. Students who answer correctly can be asked to state at what angle of incidence the reflected ray would travel back along the incident ray's path, justifying their answer.

assessment_items.stage_label: Observe and describe reflection of light
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can state the two laws of reflection and support each law with measured angle data from their own investigation, correctly identifying the normal, incident ray, and reflected ray.

competency.competency_text: Demonstrating rectilinear propagation of light from different sources and verifying the laws of reflection through manipulation of light sources and objects and the use of apparatus and artefacts such as plane mirrors, pinhole camera, kaleidoscope, and periscope.

assessment_items.question_text: State the two laws of reflection. For each law, write one sentence explaining how a student would verify it during the angle-tracing investigation with a mirror and torch.
expected_elements: First law stated: the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection.
Verification of first law: the student measures both angles with a protractor across multiple trials and confirms they are numerically equal in every trial.
Second law stated: the incident ray, the normal at the point of incidence, and the reflected ray all lie in the same plane.
Verification of second law: the student confirms that the traced incident ray, the drawn normal, and the traced reflected ray all lie flat on the same sheet of paper (the same plane).

SCR.inclusivity: Students who recall the laws but struggle with the verification language may first state the law and then describe what they physically did during the investigation — any description of measuring angles from the normal or confirming that all three lines lie on the paper counts as valid verification language. Students who complete this quickly can be asked to explain why measuring from the mirror surface rather than the normal would lead to a false conclusion about whether the first law holds.

assessment_items.stage_label: Investigate image properties in a plane mirror
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can locate the image formed by a plane mirror using the pin method, measure object and image distances, and describe the image as virtual, upright, same-size, and laterally inverted with observational evidence for each property.

competency.competency_text: Demonstrating rectilinear propagation of light from different sources and verifying the laws of reflection through manipulation of light sources and objects and the use of apparatus and artefacts such as plane mirrors, pinhole camera, kaleidoscope, and periscope.

assessment_items.question_text: A student places an object 6 cm in front of a plane mirror and uses the pin method to locate the image. Which set of properties correctly describes the image?

options.label: A
options.text: Located 12 cm behind the mirror, same size as the object, virtual, and laterally inverted.

options.label: B
options.text: Located 6 cm behind the mirror, same size as the object, virtual, and laterally inverted.

options.label: C
options.text: Located 6 cm behind the mirror, smaller than the object, virtual, and upright.

options.label: D
options.text: Located 6 cm in front of the mirror, same size as the object, real, and upright.

what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing this option shows the student has confused real and virtual images — locating the image in front of the mirror is a property of real images formed by curved mirrors, not plane mirrors — and has not applied the equal-distance result from the investigation.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Choosing this option reveals the student has the position correct (behind the mirror, equal distance) but has incorrectly attributed a size change, possibly confusing plane mirror behaviour with curved mirror behaviour.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing this option shows the student has doubled the distance, a common arithmetic error suggesting the student may be confusing total object-to-image distance (12 cm) with image distance from the mirror (6 cm).

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who struggle with multiple simultaneous properties may be invited to answer one property at a time: position, then size, then real/virtual, then orientation. Students who answer correctly can be asked to explain why the image being virtual means it cannot be projected onto a screen.

assessment_items.stage_label: Investigate image properties in a plane mirror
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can locate the image formed by a plane mirror using the pin method, measure object and image distances, and describe the image as virtual, upright, same-size, and laterally inverted with observational evidence for each property.

competency.competency_text: Demonstrating rectilinear propagation of light from different sources and verifying the laws of reflection through manipulation of light sources and objects and the use of apparatus and artefacts such as plane mirrors, pinhole camera, kaleidoscope, and periscope.

assessment_items.question_text: The word AMBULANCE is printed in reverse on emergency vehicles so that drivers ahead can read it correctly in their rear-view mirrors. Which property of plane mirror images explains why this works?

options.label: A
options.text: Equal image distance — because the image is as far behind the mirror as the ambulance is in front, the word appears at the right distance to read.

options.label: B
options.text: Inversion — the plane mirror flips the word upside down, and since the original word is reversed, the double flip produces a readable image.

options.label: C
options.text: Lateral inversion — the plane mirror reverses the left and right sides of the image, making a reversed word appear as the correct word in the mirror.

options.label: D
options.text: Virtual image — because the image is behind the mirror it cannot be projected, so the driver sees a correct image without distortion.

what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing this option shows the student has recalled the virtual image property but applied it to the wrong phenomenon — the AMBULANCE effect is about reversal of left and right, not about projectability.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing this option reveals the student has recalled the equal-distance property but cannot connect it to the AMBULANCE phenomenon, indicating recall without application.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Choosing this option reveals a confusion between lateral inversion (left-right reversal) and vertical inversion, suggesting the student is conflating plane mirror properties with the inverted image of the pinhole camera.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who struggle with the abstract AMBULANCE example may be invited to write a short word on paper, hold it in front of a mirror, and observe the result before answering. Students who answer correctly can be asked to name one other real-world application of lateral inversion from the chapter or from their own experience.

assessment_items.stage_label: Investigate image properties in a plane mirror
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can locate the image formed by a plane mirror using the pin method, measure object and image distances, and describe the image as virtual, upright, same-size, and laterally inverted with observational evidence for each property.

competency.competency_text: Demonstrating rectilinear propagation of light from different sources and verifying the laws of reflection through manipulation of light sources and objects and the use of apparatus and artefacts such as plane mirrors, pinhole camera, kaleidoscope, and periscope.

assessment_items.question_text: A student places an object pin 8 cm in front of a plane mirror. Using the pin method, they locate the image. (a) State where the image is located and how far it is from the mirror. (b) The student tries to catch the image on a white screen held behind the mirror. What will the student observe, and what does this tell us about the nature of the image?
expected_elements: Statement that the image is located behind the mirror at a distance of 8 cm from the mirror surface.
Statement that no image will be formed on the screen — the screen will appear blank or uniformly lit.

Conclusion that this shows the image is virtual — it cannot be projected onto a screen because the reflected rays only appear to diverge from a point behind the mirror but do not actually converge there.

SCR.inclusivity: Students who struggle to articulate the virtual image definition may describe the observation (nothing on screen) and leave the formal term implied; a response that clearly states the screen shows nothing and links this to the rays not actually converging is sufficient. Students who complete both parts quickly can be asked to contrast this result with what would happen if a pinhole camera were pointed at the same object — where would the image appear and could it be caught on the screen inside the camera?

assessment_items.stage_label: Demonstrate and verify behaviour of light through systematic manipulation of apparatus
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can demonstrate that light travels in straight lines and verify the laws of reflection by manipulating light sources, mirrors, and optical apparatus — including pinhole cameras, plane mirrors, and kaleidoscopes — and justify each predicted outcome using the appropriate physical principle.

competency.competency_text: Demonstrating rectilinear propagation of light from different sources and verifying the laws of reflection through manipulation of light sources and objects and the use of apparatus and artefacts such as plane mirrors, pinhole camera, kaleidoscope, and periscope.

assessment_items.question_text: A student places an object between two plane mirrors held at 90 degrees and counts the images. The student then reduces the angle to 45 degrees. Which prediction is correct, and which principle best explains it?

options.label: A
options.text: The number of images decreases when the angle is reduced to 45 degrees, because there is less space between the mirrors for images to form.

options.label: B
options.text: The number of images increases, because the smaller angle means the mirrors are almost parallel and light bends more easily between them.

options.label: C
options.text: The number of images increases when the angle is reduced to 45 degrees, because a smaller angle allows more repeated reflections between the two mirrors.

options.label: D
options.text: The number of images stays the same, because the object itself has not changed and each mirror still produces one image.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing this option reveals a spatial-intuition error: the student is thinking about physical space rather than the number of times the reflected beams can bounce back and forth between the two mirror surfaces.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing this option shows the student has treated each mirror independently rather than understanding that the two mirrors interact — reflected rays from one mirror become incident rays on the other, generating additional images.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Choosing this option reveals a correct prediction but an incorrect explanation that reintroduces the bending misconception, indicating the student has not connected multiple reflections to the laws of reflection and straight-line travel.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who struggle to visualise the geometry may set up two books as stand-ins for mirrors at the stated angles before answering. Students who answer correctly can be challenged to predict the number of images at 60 degrees (the kaleidoscope angle) and connect this to the symmetry they observed when building the kaleidoscope.

assessment_items.stage_label: Demonstrate and verify behaviour of light through systematic manipulation of apparatus
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can demonstrate that light travels in straight lines and verify the laws of reflection by manipulating light sources, mirrors, and optical apparatus — including pinhole cameras, plane mirrors, and kaleidoscopes — and justify each predicted outcome using the appropriate physical principle.

competency.competency_text: Demonstrating rectilinear propagation of light from different sources and verifying the laws of reflection through manipulation of light sources and objects and the use of apparatus and artefacts such as plane mirrors, pinhole camera, kaleidoscope, and periscope.

assessment_items.question_text: A periscope uses two plane mirrors, each tilted at 45 degrees, to allow a person to see over a wall. Which statement correctly explains how the periscope works using the laws of reflection?

options.label: A
options.text: Light bends around the wall and enters the lower mirror directly, where the 45-degree mirror straightens the beam toward the eye.

options.label: B
options.text: Light from above the wall strikes the upper mirror at 45 degrees and is reflected downward at 45 degrees to the lower mirror, which reflects it horizontally to the eye, with each angle of reflection equalling its angle of incidence.

options.label: C
options.text: Light travels in a curve between the two mirrors because the 45-degree angle causes gradual deflection rather than a sharp bounce.

options.label: D
options.text: The two mirrors face each other and produce multiple images, one of which happens to be visible over the wall.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing this option reveals the bending misconception applied to the periscope context — the student has not applied rectilinear propagation to explain how light enters the device from above.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing this option shows the student has confused the periscope (two mirrors at 45°, each reflecting once) with the multiple-reflection two-mirror investigation, applying the wrong concept from the chapter.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Choosing this option reveals the misconception that reflection produces a gradual curve rather than an abrupt direction change governed by the equal-angle law — a direct contradiction of both laws of reflection.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who struggle with the three-dimensional geometry of the periscope may sketch a side view showing the wall, the two mirrors, and the path of light before choosing an answer. Students who answer correctly can be asked to identify which property of the plane mirror image (virtual, laterally inverted, same size) applies to what a person sees when they look into a periscope.
