assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can demonstrate that light travels in straight lines and verify the laws of reflection by manipulating light sources, mirrors, and optical apparatus — including pinhole cameras, plane mirrors, and kaleidoscopes — and justify each predicted outcome using the appropriate physical principle.

competency.competency_text: Demonstrating rectilinear propagation of light from different sources and verifying the laws of reflection through manipulation of light sources and objects and the use of apparatus and artefacts such as plane mirrors, pinhole camera, kaleidoscope, and periscope.

assessment_items.question_text: Across this chapter, you have used three different pieces of apparatus: the three-card alignment setup, the pinhole camera, and the plane mirror with the angle-tracing investigation. Choose any two of these and explain, for each, (a) what you did with the apparatus, (b) what result you observed, and (c) which physical principle — rectilinear propagation or a law of reflection — the result supports and why.
look_for: For each chosen apparatus: a clear, accurate description of the manipulation performed (e.g. aligning or misaligning the holes; pointing the camera at a bright object; directing a ray at the mirror at a measured angle).
For each chosen apparatus: a specific, accurate statement of the observed result (e.g. flame disappears when any card is misaligned; inverted image forms on the screen; measured angles are equal).

For each chosen apparatus: an explicit and correctly chosen physical principle (rectilinear propagation for the card setup and pinhole camera; first law of reflection for the angle-tracing investigation).
For each chosen apparatus: a causal justification explaining why the observation supports the named principle — not merely asserting that it does.
Responses that connect the two chosen apparatus to different principles demonstrate higher-order understanding of the chapter's dual themes.

ECR.inclusivity: Students who find extended writing difficult may respond using a two-column table — one column for each apparatus chosen — with rows for what they did, what they observed, and which principle applies. Students who demonstrate strong causal reasoning for two apparatus can be invited to add a third and address whether any apparatus from the chapter could test both principles in a single investigation.

assessment_items.stage_label: Demonstrate and verify behaviour of light through systematic manipulation of apparatus
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can demonstrate that light travels in straight lines and verify the laws of reflection by manipulating light sources, mirrors, and optical apparatus — including pinhole cameras, plane mirrors, and kaleidoscopes — and justify each predicted outcome using the appropriate physical principle.

competency.competency_text: Demonstrating rectilinear propagation of light from different sources and verifying the laws of reflection through manipulation of light sources, mirrors, and optical apparatus.

assessment_items.visual_stimulus:
Apparatus setup | Observation | Principle being tested | Setup change | Predicted new observation | Justification
Three cards aligned, candle at one end | Candle flame visible through all holes | | Shift the middle card 2 cm sideways | | 
Pinhole camera pointed at a bright lamp | Inverted image on screen | | Make the pinhole three times larger | | 
Plane mirror, ray at 30° to the normal | Reflected ray at 30° to the normal | | Change the angle of incidence to 50° | | 
Two mirrors at 90°, small object between them | Three images visible | | Reduce the angle to 45° | |
assessment_items.task: Refer to the table provided. Each row describes an apparatus setup and an initial observation. For each row: (1) name the principle being tested; (2) predict the new observation after the stated change; (3) justify your prediction using that principle.
assessment_items.scaffold: For each row, ask yourself: which physical principle — rectilinear propagation or a law of reflection — governs this setup? Then trace through what the stated change does to the light path or angle, and write what you would expect to see. Your justification should explain the causal link between the principle and your prediction.
format_of_output: Completed table with the three empty columns filled in for all four rows.
Each justification written as one or two sentences using the vocabulary of the chapter — ray, normal, angle of incidence, angle of reflection, straight line, reflection.

OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The final stage's implied LO requires students to both demonstrate and justify light behaviour using systematic manipulation of apparatus; a predict-and-explain task directly requires the student to apply the physical principle to an unfamiliar change in each apparatus setup, which is the most natural demonstration vehicle for this LO.
OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: A complete response evidences the student's ability to identify the governing physical principle for each apparatus, apply it to predict an outcome under a changed condition, and articulate the causal mechanism — the highest cognitive demand of the chapter.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold is a prompt to sequence the student's reasoning: identify the principle first, then trace the effect of the change, then predict. Teachers should look for whether students are applying the principle generatively (predicting from understanding) or guessing — strong responses will have specific causal language such as 'the straight-line path is broken' or 'by the first law the new reflected angle must also be 50°'.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong responses: correct principle named for all four rows; predictions that follow necessarily from the principle; justifications that name specific features of the changed setup (e.g. 'a larger pinhole allows rays from many angles to reach the same screen point'). Weak responses: correct predictions without causal justification, or justifications that merely restate the observation without connecting it to a principle.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who struggle with the full table may be asked to complete any two rows of their choice; partial completion that demonstrates deep causal reasoning on two rows is more informative than shallow completion of all four. Students who complete all four rows fluently can be challenged to design a fifth row of their own — a new apparatus change — and predict and justify its outcome.
